prompt: A developer wants to know where a function was written. Which kind of feature answers that?
optionA: One that lists every place the name is used
optionB: One that jumps to where a name is defined
optionC: One that searches the project for matching text
optionD: One that renames the name everywhere
correctAnswerText: One that jumps to where a name is defined
explanation: Finding the definition and finding the uses are opposite questions. A text search would find both and force the developer to sort them out by eye.

prompt: A developer wants to know everywhere a function is called before changing it. Which kind of feature answers that?
optionA: One that jumps to where the name is defined
optionB: One that renames the name everywhere
optionC: One that reformats the file
optionD: One that reports every place the name is used
correctAnswerText: One that reports every place the name is used
explanation: The question is about uses rather than the definition. Renaming would change them rather than reporting them.

prompt: A developer wants to find every place a particular phrase appears in comments. Which kind of feature answers that?
optionA: One that searches for matching text
optionB: One that jumps to where a name is defined
optionC: One that reports where a name is used
optionD: One that renames a name everywhere
correctAnswerText: One that searches for matching text
explanation: Comments carry no meaning the tool understands, so a text search is the right instrument. The meaning-aware features would ignore them entirely.

prompt: What distinguishes a text search from a search that understands the code?
optionA: One is faster than the other
optionB: One works on saved files and the other on open ones
optionC: One matches characters and the other matches the thing a name refers to
optionD: One is case sensitive and the other is not
correctAnswerText: One matches characters and the other matches the thing a name refers to
explanation: A text search finds a name inside a comment and inside a longer word. A meaning-aware search finds the specific thing and skips coincidental matches.

prompt: A developer uses a text search to find every call to a function named "run" and receives hundreds of results. What accounts for that?
optionA: The function really is called hundreds of times
optionB: The text appears inside longer words, comments and unrelated names
optionC: The search covered too many directories
optionD: The search was case insensitive
correctAnswerText: The text appears inside longer words, comments and unrelated names
explanation: A short common name matches a great deal of text that has nothing to do with it. A meaning-aware usage report would have found only the calls.

prompt: A project-wide search returns no results for a name. What does that establish?
optionA: That the name does not appear in the project
optionB: That the name has been deleted
optionC: That the name was never used
optionD: That the name was not found in what the search covered
correctAnswerText: That the name was not found in what the search covered
explanation: A search reports on what it looked at. What it looked at is a separate question with its own answer.

prompt: A project excludes a directory of generated files from searching. A name used only there is searched for. What is reported?
optionA: No results, because the excluded directory was not examined
optionB: The uses in the excluded directory
optionC: A warning that a directory was skipped
optionD: An error, since the name exists
correctAnswerText: No results, because the excluded directory was not examined
explanation: Exclusions are silent by design, so the search simply reports nothing. Knowing what is excluded is what makes an empty result interpretable.

prompt: Which question does an empty search result answer?
optionA: Whether the text exists anywhere in the project
optionB: Whether the text was ever used
optionC: Whether the text was found in the searched files
optionD: Whether the code compiles
correctAnswerText: Whether the text was found in the searched files
explanation: The result is about the files examined and nothing beyond them. Widening the claim is where the mistake gets made.

prompt: A developer searches for a function name, finds no results, and deletes the function as unused. It breaks the build. What did the search fail to cover?
optionA: The definition of the function itself
optionB: Somewhere the name is used that the search did not examine
optionC: The comments in the project
optionD: The most recently edited files
correctAnswerText: Somewhere the name is used that the search did not examine
explanation: Something used the function and the search did not look there — an excluded directory, a configuration file, or a name assembled at run time. The empty result was accurate and narrower than it appeared.

prompt: A line is underlined in an editor with a note suggesting a shorter way to write it. What kind of claim is that?
optionA: A statement that the code will fail
optionB: A statement that the code will not compile
optionC: A statement that the code has been tested
optionD: A style suggestion, not a statement that the code is wrong
correctAnswerText: A style suggestion, not a statement that the code is wrong
explanation: Suggestions about how something is written are separate from claims that it is broken. Both appear as underlines and mean different things.

prompt: A marker reports that a name cannot be found. What kind of claim is that?
optionA: That the tool could not resolve the name, which usually means the code will not build
optionB: That the code is badly written
optionC: That the code is slow
optionD: That the code has not been saved
correctAnswerText: That the tool could not resolve the name, which usually means the code will not build
explanation: An unresolvable name is a claim about correctness rather than style. It is the kind of marker worth acting on immediately.

prompt: Two editors show different markers on the same file. What does that indicate?
optionA: That one of the two is faulty
optionB: That the file changed between the two
optionC: That the two are checking for different things
optionD: That one editor is a newer version
correctAnswerText: That the two are checking for different things
explanation: A marker is one tool opinion, and different tools hold different opinions. Neither is a property of the code itself.

prompt: A developer treats every underline in their editor as something that must be removed before committing. What is the weakness?
optionA: Nothing; a clean file is always better
optionB: Style suggestions and genuine faults are being treated as one thing
optionC: Underlines cannot be removed
optionD: The editor will re-add them anyway
correctAnswerText: Style suggestions and genuine faults are being treated as one thing
explanation: Some markers report code that will not build and others express a preference. Treating them alike either wastes time or lets a real fault through in the noise.

prompt: A developer follows a function name to its definition and arrives somewhere. What has the tool done?
optionA: Searched the project for matching text
optionB: Guessed based on the file currently open
optionC: Taken them to the first definition alphabetically
optionD: Taken them to where it worked out the name is defined
correctAnswerText: Taken them to where it worked out the name is defined
explanation: The jump rests on the tool understanding of the code. That understanding can be wrong, which is why the destination is worth glancing at.

prompt: Two different modules each define a function with the same name, and a developer follows one call. What determines where they land?
optionA: Which definition the tool has worked out this call refers to
optionB: Which definition appears first in the project
optionC: Which file was most recently edited
optionD: Which module has the shorter name
correctAnswerText: Which definition the tool has worked out this call refers to
explanation: The tool resolves the call the way the language would, and lands on that one. Where two definitions genuinely could apply, some tools offer a choice instead.

prompt: A usage report lists eight places a function is called. What does it establish?
optionA: That the function is called exactly eight times
optionB: That the function is called from eight files
optionC: That the tool found eight; whether there are others depends on what it could see
optionD: That the function is safe to change
correctAnswerText: That the tool found eight; whether there are others depends on what it could see
explanation: The report covers what the tool understood. Calls constructed at run time or made from configuration are outside what it can resolve.

prompt: A project calls some functions by name assembled from a string at run time. A usage report for one such function shows no results. What follows?
optionA: The function is genuinely unused
optionB: The report cannot see calls of that kind, so the absence proves nothing
optionC: The report has failed and should be run again
optionD: The function is called from a different project
correctAnswerText: The report cannot see calls of that kind, so the absence proves nothing
explanation: A name that only exists as text at run time is invisible to a meaning-aware search. A plain text search would find the string.

prompt: A developer renames a function through the editor. What is changed?
optionA: Every occurrence of that text in the project
optionB: The definition only
optionC: The definition and the uses in the open file only
optionD: The definition and every use the tool recognised
correctAnswerText: The definition and every use the tool recognised
explanation: The rename follows the tool understanding of what refers to what. A text-based replacement would change every occurrence including coincidental ones.

prompt: A function name also appears in a comment and in a configuration file. A rename is performed through the editor. What happens to those two?
optionA: Both are left unchanged, since neither is a use the tool recognises
optionB: Both are updated along with the code
optionC: The comment is updated and the configuration file is not
optionD: The configuration file is updated and the comment is not
correctAnswerText: Both are left unchanged, since neither is a use the tool recognises
explanation: Neither a comment nor a configuration entry is code the tool resolves. Both have to be found and changed separately.

prompt: A developer renames a class through the editor, the project builds cleanly, and the application fails at start-up. The class name appears in a configuration file that is read at run time, and a rename changes only what the tool recognises as code. What happened?
optionA: The rename missed some of the code
optionB: The build succeeded incorrectly
optionC: The configuration still names the old class, and nothing checked it at build time
optionD: The new name conflicts with an existing one
correctAnswerText: The configuration still names the old class, and nothing checked it at build time
explanation: Building cleanly is exactly what makes this hard to anticipate. The configuration is read at run time and nothing connects it to the rename.

prompt: A terminal is opened inside an editor. Which directory does it usually start in?
optionA: The directory of the file currently open
optionB: The root of the project being edited
optionC: The user home directory
optionD: The directory where the editor is installed
correctAnswerText: The root of the project being edited
explanation: The project root is the common convention, and it need not match the open file. Which one a given tool uses is worth checking rather than assuming.

prompt: A file is open at a path several directories below the project root, and a terminal is opened inside the editor. A relative path that works when running from the file own directory is typed in. What happens?
optionA: It resolves from the file directory as intended
optionB: The terminal refuses the path
optionC: The terminal moves to the file directory automatically
optionD: It resolves from the project root instead and does not reach the intended file
correctAnswerText: It resolves from the project root instead and does not reach the intended file
explanation: The terminal location and the open file location are independent. A relative path is resolved from wherever the terminal actually is.

prompt: A command works when typed into the editor terminal and fails when a colleague runs the identical command from their own shell. The command contains a relative path and the two terminals were started in different directories. What is the cause?
optionA: The relative path resolves from a different directory in each case
optionB: The colleague lacks permission on the file
optionC: The editor modifies the command before running it
optionD: The command depends on the editor being open
correctAnswerText: The relative path resolves from a different directory in each case
explanation: The command line is identical and what it names is not. Using a path from the project root, or moving to a known directory first, removes the dependence.

prompt: A developer presses run in an editor. What executes the code?
optionA: The editor itself
optionB: The operating system directly
optionC: An interpreter or compiler installed separately, chosen by a setting
optionD: Whichever tool was used to write the code
correctAnswerText: An interpreter or compiler installed separately, chosen by a setting
explanation: The editor hands the work to something else and displays the result. Which something is a configuration choice.

prompt: Three versions of a language are installed on a machine. Which one runs the code when the developer presses run?
optionA: The newest installed version
optionB: Whichever the project or editor setting names
optionC: The oldest installed version
optionD: Whichever was installed most recently
correctAnswerText: Whichever the project or editor setting names
explanation: A setting decides, and it may name a version quite unlike what the developer expects. Nothing about being newest gives a version priority.

prompt: A developer installs a library and the editor still reports that it cannot be found when the code runs. The library was installed into one environment and the editor is configured to run the code with a different one. What is the cause?
optionA: The library failed to install
optionB: The editor needs restarting to see new libraries
optionC: The library is incompatible with the code
optionD: The library and the run configuration point at different environments
correctAnswerText: The library and the run configuration point at different environments
explanation: The install succeeded and put the library somewhere the running code never looks. Pointing the run configuration at the same environment resolves it.

prompt: A file shows no markers of any kind. What does that establish about running it?
optionA: Nothing; the tool found nothing it checks for
optionB: That it will run correctly
optionC: That it will compile and run without error
optionD: That it has been tested
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the tool found nothing it checks for
explanation: A clean file means the checks the tool performs found nothing. Whether the code does the right thing is not among those checks.

prompt: A file shows several markers and the program runs correctly. Is that contradictory?
optionA: Yes; a marked file cannot run correctly
optionB: Yes; the program must be failing silently
optionC: No; markers may report style preferences or checks the running code does not depend on
optionD: No, but only because the markers are stale
correctAnswerText: No; markers may report style preferences or checks the running code does not depend on
explanation: Plenty of markers report things that are not errors. The program running says nothing about whether the suggestions were worth taking.

prompt: A program fails when run, and the developer looks for a marked line to explain it. The file shows no markers at all. The tool reports nothing and the program failed at run time on something the tool does not check. What follows?
optionA: The tool has failed to update its markers
optionB: The fault is of a kind the tool does not examine, so the markers cannot help here
optionC: The program failure must be unrelated to the code
optionD: The file must be reopened for the markers to appear
correctAnswerText: The fault is of a kind the tool does not examine, so the markers cannot help here
explanation: Most run-time faults — a wrong value, a missing file, a bad assumption — are invisible to a tool reading the code. Looking to the markers for them is looking in the wrong place.

prompt: A developer installs an extension giving their editor knowledge of a language. What has become possible?
optionA: The language is now installed and can run code
optionB: Code in that language will now compile
optionC: The editor can run the code without anything else
optionD: The editor can understand and check code in that language
correctAnswerText: The editor can understand and check code in that language
explanation: The extension teaches the editor about the language. Running the code needs the language itself, installed separately.

prompt: A developer installs a language extension, writes code, and finds the editor understands it perfectly while pressing run produces an error saying the command is not found. What is missing?
optionA: The language itself, which the extension does not install
optionB: A second extension for running code
optionC: A restart of the editor
optionD: A project configuration file
correctAnswerText: The language itself, which the extension does not install
explanation: The two capabilities come from different places and are easy to conflate. Understanding the code and being able to execute it are separate installations.

prompt: A developer opens a file in a language for which no extension is installed. No markers appear anywhere in the file. Without an extension the editor has no knowledge of the language, so it has nothing to check the file against. What does the absence of markers establish?
optionA: That the file is free of errors
optionB: That the file is empty
optionC: Nothing at all; the editor has nothing to check the file against
optionD: That the file will run correctly
correctAnswerText: Nothing at all; the editor has nothing to check the file against
explanation: This is the strongest form of the trap: a clean file that has not been examined. Installing the extension often produces a page of markers on the same unchanged file.

prompt: A marker reports that a name cannot be found. The developer has just created that name in another file. What is the likely explanation?
optionA: The name was created incorrectly
optionB: The tool has not re-examined the project since the name was created
optionC: The name must be created in the same file
optionD: The tool has found a second name with the same spelling
correctAnswerText: The tool has not re-examined the project since the name was created
explanation: The tool reports what was true when it last looked. Prompting it to re-examine the project is the usual remedy.

prompt: A developer changes correct code to remove a marker, and the program stops working. The marker described the code as it had been several edits earlier and no longer applied. What went wrong?
optionA: The marker was accurate and the change was made incorrectly
optionB: The program failure is unrelated to the change
optionC: The marker should have been reported as an error rather than a warning
optionD: The marker was out of date and the code it described had already been corrected
correctAnswerText: The marker was out of date and the code it described had already been corrected
explanation: Editing working code to satisfy a stale claim is the expensive direction of this fault. Confirming that the marker still applies before acting on it is what prevents it.

prompt: Code runs correctly from a terminal and fails in the editor with an error about a missing library. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The editor is running the code with a different environment from the terminal
optionB: The library was never installed
optionC: The editor cannot run code with libraries
optionD: The code is different in the two cases
correctAnswerText: The editor is running the code with a different environment from the terminal
explanation: The same code succeeding in one place and failing in another points at what is running it. The library exists somewhere, or the terminal run would have failed too.

prompt: A developer follows an installation instruction, sees it report success, and the editor still cannot find the library. The install ran in one environment and the editor is configured to use another, and both are present on the machine. What should they check?
optionA: Whether the install genuinely succeeded
optionB: Whether the library supports their operating system
optionC: Which environment the editor is configured to use, and whether the install went to that one
optionD: Whether the editor needs reinstalling
correctAnswerText: Which environment the editor is configured to use, and whether the install went to that one
explanation: Both reports are accurate about different environments. Making the install and the run configuration agree is the whole of the fix.

prompt: A tool that checks for unused variables reports nothing on a file. What has been established?
optionA: That the file has no problems
optionB: That it found no unused variables
optionC: That every variable is used correctly
optionD: That the file is well written
correctAnswerText: That it found no unused variables
explanation: The claim is exactly as wide as what the tool checks. Everything outside that remains unexamined.

prompt: A team runs three tools over a file and all report nothing. They conclude the file is correct. The three tools between them check formatting, unused names and type consistency, and none examines whether the logic is right. What has been established?
optionA: That the file is correct
optionB: That the file has no faults of any kind
optionC: Nothing, since automated tools are unreliable
optionD: That the file passes those three kinds of check, which do not include whether it does the right thing
correctAnswerText: That the file passes those three kinds of check, which do not include whether it does the right thing
explanation: Three narrow checks passing is genuinely worth something and is not a verdict on behaviour. Tests are what examine whether the code does what was wanted.

prompt: A developer relies on the absence of markers as their only check before committing. Their editor has no extension installed for one of the languages in the project. Files in that language are never examined, and their cleanliness is indistinguishable from a file that has passed every check. What is the position?
optionA: Files in that language pass unchecked, and nothing in the editor distinguishes them from checked ones
optionB: All files are checked equally
optionC: Files in that language will show an error about the missing extension
optionD: The editor will refuse to open files it cannot check
correctAnswerText: Files in that language pass unchecked, and nothing in the editor distinguishes them from checked ones
explanation: The absence of a marker means the same thing visually whether the file passed or was never looked at. A check that runs outside the editor removes the ambiguity.

prompt: A team adds a rule that no code may be committed while any marker is showing. Some markers report genuine faults and others express style preferences that the team disagrees with. The rule treats a preference the team rejects and a genuine fault as equally blocking. What will happen?
optionA: Every genuine fault will be fixed before committing
optionB: The style preferences will gradually be adopted
optionC: People will silence the preferences they disagree with, and the habit will extend to genuine faults
optionD: Nothing; the rule is unambiguous and workable
correctAnswerText: People will silence the preferences they disagree with, and the habit will extend to genuine faults
explanation: A rule that blocks on things the team considers wrong teaches people to suppress markers. Configuring the tool to stop reporting the unwanted preferences keeps the rule meaningful.

prompt: A developer notices that a tool stops reporting a particular kind of problem after a configuration change somebody made months ago. The tool has been silent on that check since the change, and silence looks identical whether a check is passing or disabled. What follows about the intervening months?
optionA: The problems were fixed, which is why reporting stopped
optionB: Nothing was being checked, and every clean report since then said less than it appeared to
optionC: The tool has been failing and should be reinstalled
optionD: The check was reporting nothing because there was nothing to report
correctAnswerText: Nothing was being checked, and every clean report since then said less than it appeared to
explanation: A disabled check and a passing check produce the same silence. Reviewing what is enabled is the only way to tell one from the other.

prompt: A developer must find every place a method is called before changing its signature. The method has a common name that also appears in comments and inside longer words. The question is about calls to one specific method rather than about occurrences of the text. Which approach fits?
optionA: A text search for the method name
optionB: A text search restricted to one directory
optionC: Reading each file in the project
optionD: A usage report, which resolves the name rather than matching the text
correctAnswerText: A usage report, which resolves the name rather than matching the text
explanation: The text search would return a great deal that has nothing to do with the method. Reading every file would work and is the slowest route available.

prompt: A developer must find every place a configuration key is referenced. The key is named as a string in code and in several configuration files. The key exists only as text and is never a name the tool resolves. Which approach fits?
optionA: A text search, since the key is text everywhere it appears
optionB: A usage report, which understands the code
optionC: Following the key to its definition
optionD: Renaming the key and seeing what breaks
correctAnswerText: A text search, since the key is text everywhere it appears
explanation: Meaning-aware features resolve names in code and a string is not one. Renaming to see what breaks would work and destroys the running system to answer a question.

prompt: A developer must rename something referenced both as code and as a string in configuration. The name appears both as code the tool resolves and as text in files it does not. What approach fits?
optionA: The rename feature alone, which handles both
optionB: A text replacement alone, which handles both
optionC: The rename feature for the code, followed by a text search for the remaining occurrences
optionD: Neither; the name should not be changed
correctAnswerText: The rename feature for the code, followed by a text search for the remaining occurrences
explanation: Each instrument covers one half and neither covers both. A text replacement alone would also change coincidental matches inside longer words.

prompt: A developer can spend ten minutes learning a feature that would answer this question in seconds, or twenty minutes answering it by hand. They will face this question several times a week. The question recurs several times a week and the feature answers it in seconds. What follows?
optionA: Answer it by hand, since twenty minutes is not long
optionB: Learn the feature, since the cost is paid once and the saving recurs
optionC: Answer it by hand this time and learn the feature later
optionD: Neither; the question should be avoided
correctAnswerText: Learn the feature, since the cost is paid once and the saving recurs
explanation: A one-off cost against a recurring saving is settled by the recurrence. For a question asked once, doing it by hand would be the right answer.

prompt: A developer needs to know what a program actually does at a particular point. They can read the code carefully or run it and observe. The code is short and calls into several libraries whose behaviour they do not know. Reading the code would require understanding libraries they have never used. Which fits?
optionA: Reading it carefully, since reading is always more reliable
optionB: Reading it carefully, since the code is short
optionC: Neither; they should ask a colleague
optionD: Running it and observing, since reading requires knowledge they do not have
correctAnswerText: Running it and observing, since reading requires knowledge they do not have
explanation: Reading is the better route when the code is self-contained, and here it is not. The length of the code is not what makes it readable.

prompt: An unfamiliar tool advertises a check that reports every function never called from anywhere in the project. It reports three functions. The check examines calls it can resolve within the project and cannot see calls made from outside it. What has it established?
optionA: That three functions have no resolvable call within the project, which is narrower than being unused
optionB: That three functions are unused and can be deleted
optionC: That the project contains only three unnecessary functions
optionD: Nothing; such checks are unreliable
correctAnswerText: That three functions have no resolvable call within the project, which is narrower than being unused
explanation: Functions called from another project, from configuration or by name at run time are outside what it can see. The report is genuinely useful as a list of candidates to investigate.

prompt: An unfamiliar tool offers to apply a fix automatically wherever it finds a particular pattern. A developer applies it across a large project. The tool applies its change wherever the pattern matches, without regard to whether each match was intended to be that way. What should they do before accepting?
optionA: Accept it, since the tool found genuine matches
optionB: Accept it, since automatic fixes are tested by their authors
optionC: Review what it changed, since a matching pattern is not always a mistake
optionD: Reject it, since automatic fixes are never safe
correctAnswerText: Review what it changed, since a matching pattern is not always a mistake
explanation: The tool is right about the pattern and cannot know which occurrences were deliberate. Reviewing the change is the step that separates the two.

prompt: A developer moves to an unfamiliar editor and finds that a search returns far fewer results than the same search in their previous one. The new editor excludes files listed as ignored by the project, and the previous one did not. Which is right?
optionA: The previous editor, since more results is more complete
optionB: Neither; the two are answering different questions and the developer has to know which they want
optionC: The new editor, since ignored files should not be searched
optionD: The new editor, since fewer results are easier to read
correctAnswerText: Neither; the two are answering different questions and the developer has to know which they want
explanation: Searching generated files is sometimes exactly what is wanted and sometimes noise. Knowing which behaviour a tool has is what makes an empty result interpretable.

prompt: A team must decide whether their agreed checks should run in the editor, in a step everyone runs before committing, or both. Editor checks give immediate feedback and can be configured away individually, while a shared step runs the same way for everyone. Immediate feedback is per-developer and configurable, and the shared step is identical for everyone. Which fits a team that needs the checks actually applied?
optionA: The editor alone, since feedback is most useful while writing
optionB: The shared step alone, since it is the one that counts
optionC: Either, since the checks are the same
optionD: Both, with the shared step as the one that decides and the editor as the one that gives feedback early
correctAnswerText: Both, with the shared step as the one that decides and the editor as the one that gives feedback early
explanation: Each covers what the other cannot: the editor is fast and optional, the shared step is authoritative and late. Choosing one gives up either the speed or the guarantee.
